title: A multiplexed biochemical flight recorder for living cells

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an internal molecular recorder that stores a history of many biochemical activities in an individual living cell for later readout. Instead of requiring continuous observation, it would preserve enough information to reconstruct which events occurred, their order, their timing and their approximate strength. The intended advance combines diverse biochemical coverage, useful temporal accuracy, long recording periods and limited disturbance of the cell. This combination is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

CytoTape provides a concrete technical foundation: selected gene-regulatory activities are recorded in intracellular protein assemblies and read retrospectively. Extending that approach to a broader biochemical history requires distinguishing measurement targets. Promoter activity, transcription-factor activity, endogenous mRNA abundance and metabolic activity describe different aspects of cell behavior; recording one does not automatically measure the others. A useful general recorder would need calibrated ways to sense and distinguish its chosen targets.

The measurement problem is a trade-off among coverage, time and access. Static measurements can provide rich molecular information while losing the preceding history; continuous imaging requires sustained observation; engineered molecular recorders capture selected signals. The reviewed CytoTape study advances multiplexed, long-duration transcriptional recording, but its documented limits leave substantial room for broader biochemical coverage. The supplied materials do not establish whether the full proposed combination remains unmet across the entire field in November 2026.

significance.text: If the proposed breadth and fidelity were achieved, transient cellular histories could become accessible after the events themselves had disappeared, including in tissues where continuous microscopy is difficult. The revolutionary step would be a substantial expansion in the diversity and quantitative reliability of recorded activities. Retrospective recording itself already has a demonstrated basis: the reviewed CytoTape work includes recording in mouse brain.

A recorder could connect earlier molecular events with later cell states, provided the history can be assigned to the correct cell and combined with compatible endpoint measurements. Such connections could help identify sequences of activity associated with later responses or outcomes. Temporal association would not establish causation: interventions and mechanistic experiments would still be needed. The CytoTape discussion likewise separates recorded relationships from causal investigations.

Conditional synthesis: broader recording could help researchers investigate development, adaptation, disease progression or treatment response by comparing cells with different molecular histories. These possibilities depend on the recorder retaining relevant events without materially changing them. The flight-recorder analogy has limits: a molecular device would sample a defined set of signals with finite capacity and imperfect timing, rather than preserve every event inside a cell.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a calibrated, multiplexed history of diverse biochemical activities within the same individual cell. CytoTape's reviewed limitations include its restriction to transcriptional readouts, and its five-signal multiplexing does not establish comprehensive biochemical coverage. Extending recording to signaling and metabolic events requires more than adding transcriptional reporters: the recorded quantity must be shown to represent the intended biochemical activity.

Timing must also be established at the level of reconstructed biological events. CytoTape distinguishes timestamp transitions from the time axis inferred between them. Its supplementary discussion acknowledges uncertainty introduced by interpolation. A general recorder therefore needs evidence that event onset, duration and order can be recovered with known errors across its recording interval; resolving closely spaced timestamp changes alone does not establish that performance.

Engineering synthesis: a broader system must couple diverse molecular sensors to distinguishable storage channels, control cross-talk and characterize how sensor response and writing delays affect reconstructed histories. It must also determine when signal magnitude can be recovered rather than merely event presence. Storage turnover, saturation, cell growth or division, and the recovery of cell identity are practical boundaries to characterize wherever they apply. Increasing recording duration or channel count is useful only if the stored information remains interpretable.

Engineering synthesis: low disturbance must be demonstrated alongside information quality. Sensors, storage assemblies and readout preparation can impose burdens or alter the processes being measured. The challenge is to retain sufficient sensitivity and recording capacity while showing that the recorder does not substantially distort the relevant cell behavior. Acceptable disturbance will depend on the intended experiment and cell system.

current_state.text: The CytoTape study dated 26 January 2026 reported selected gene-regulatory histories over periods of up to three weeks. The reviewed text describes 21-day neuronal recordings with sequential KCl and forskolin stimulation and reports resolution of multiple transcriptional events. It also describes five-signal multiplexing. These results support substantial progress in recording selected transcriptional histories; they do not establish comprehensive recording of signaling, metabolism and other biochemical activities together.

The timing results have different experimental scopes. CytoTape resolved dye-switching events separated by 30 minutes in HEK cells, while the multiweek neuronal experiments resolved transcriptional features on hours scales. The supplementary text reports less-than-one-day accuracy with day-scale dye switches and acknowledges uncertainty in interpolating between timestamps. These findings should not be combined into a claim of 30-minute accuracy for biological-signal reconstruction throughout a three-week experiment.

CytoTape also supplies a basis for retrospective recording in tissue through its mouse-brain demonstration. The supplied review assessed substantive article and supplementary text, but both retained extractions were truncated, some supplementary figure text was garbled, and original figures and raw data were not independently inspected. A second supplementary PDF supplied effectively no usable scientific text. The achievements summarized here are therefore reported results assessed through the available text.

The research input identifies a work titled “Recordanelles for transcriptome-wide single-cell RNA recording in human cells,” dated 21 October 2026, and attributes to it broad endogenous-mRNA sampling and preservation over several days. Although the earlier research described an abstract inspection, the supplied review found only a cookie-access message in the retained PubMed artifact. Its contents therefore do not verify the scientific identity, date, transcript coverage, duration or limitations attributed to that work. Those claims remain unconfirmed in this record; the access failure is not evidence that the reported work or results are false.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the materials support dated progress toward the concept through CytoTape, while leaving the Recordanelles claims unresolved. The supplied review contains no usable freshness-search record, so it cannot establish a comprehensive account of the field as of 1 November 2026 or the date of this record. It also supplies no basis for classifying the inaccessible Recordanelles work as a preprint or a disputed result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct blinded tests in which independently varied signaling and metabolic events generate known histories in individual cells. From the stored record alone, reconstruct event order, timing and approximate strength over a prespecified recording period. Define the event panel, number of simultaneous channels, duration, acceptable timing and magnitude errors, reconstruction success rate and tolerable physiological effects before testing. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Stored records reconstruct blinded biochemical event histories within predefined tolerances

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: compare reconstructed histories with independent measurements appropriate to each target. Include isolated events, overlapping events, different strengths and durations, and periods when no event occurs, so that missed events, false detections and channel cross-talk can be measured. Assess timing throughout the recording interval, including between timestamps, rather than relying only on timestamp-switch resolution. Where the recorder measures a proxy, establish how that proxy relates to the intended biochemical quantity.
completion_criteria.label: Reconstructed biochemical histories match independent measurements with quantified detection errors

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the demonstration across independent preparations and laboratories, report failures and exclusions, and test the cell types and tissue settings for which usefulness is claimed. Controls should quantify effects on relevant physiology and behavior. Characterize storage capacity, loss of information, readout recovery, cell-identity assignment and performance during growth or division where applicable. A convincing result would establish a reproducible operating range; finite tests would demonstrate breadth across the tested conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent preparations and laboratories establish reproducible recorder operating boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BCH-05, “Routine, comprehensive single-cell proteoform reading,” overlaps through molecular measurement within individual cells. Its focus is identifying protein forms, whereas BCH-06 focuses on preserving temporal histories. The capabilities could complement one another if a recorded history could be linked to an endpoint proteoform measurement. Neither capability substitutes for the other.

Roster-based synthesis: BCH-10, “Predict modification-dependent biochemical networks,” could use recorded histories to constrain or test dynamic network models. Recording observations is distinct from predicting network behavior or controlling it. BCH-02, “Predict biochemical function from molecular sequence and environment,” likewise concerns inference from molecular properties and context; BCH-06 would provide experimental histories that might test such predictions without itself solving that inference problem.

Roster-based synthesis: BCH-09, “Predict and control the biochemical organization of condensates,” overlaps in the potential use of engineered intracellular organization for sensing or storage. A recorder using intracellular assemblies does not by itself establish condensate behavior or solve its prediction and control. BCH-01, “General design of enzymes for new chemical reactions,” could contribute sensing or writing chemistry, but general enzyme design and temporal recording remain separate achievements.

Roster-based synthesis: BCH-03, “A self-maintaining, evolvable cell assembled from defined components,” shares the challenge of integrating engineered molecular systems with cellular function. BCH-06 could be a measurement component within such a system, but does not require constructing an entire cell. BCH-04, “A chemically plausible route from simple feedstocks to evolving heredity,” and BCH-07, “Autonomous heredity in a chemically distinct genetic polymer,” concern origins or alternative mechanisms of heredity. Storing a cellular history is distinct from establishing heritable replication and evolution.

Roster-based synthesis: BCH-08, “Resolve the nitrogenase reaction cycle during nitrogen fixation,” and BCH-11, “Routine structural reading of complex glycans,” address specialized mechanistic and structural measurement goals. A general cellular recorder would not automatically resolve catalytic intermediates or glycan structures. Recording relevant activity histories could complement those investigations only if suitable sensing and validation were developed.

unresolved_issues: The Recordanelles publication identity, date, endogenous-mRNA coverage, recording duration and limitations remain unverified from usable scientific text in the supplied artifacts.
The earlier research's claim of abstract inspection cannot be reconciled with the cookie-only artifact available to the supplied review.
The empty freshness-search record prevents a field-wide assessment of whether another system has achieved the proposed combination by November 2026.
Truncated CytoTape extractions, garbled supplementary figure text, unavailable original-figure inspection and lack of independent raw-data inspection limit the evidentiary assessment.
The event panel, channel count, recording period, acceptable errors, success rate and tolerable physiological disturbance remain to be specified for an operational completion test.
The supplied evidence does not demonstrate broad, calibrated recording of signaling and metabolic activities together with transcriptional histories in the same cell.

brief.title: A readable history of a living cell
possible: Researchers could discover what happened inside a living cell after the events had passed, without watching it continuously. An internal recorder would preserve many kinds of activity, revealing their order, timing and approximate strength.
They could recover histories from tissues that are difficult to watch through a microscope, then connect earlier events with the cell’s later condition.
why: Brief events can disappear before researchers measure them. Preserving those events could help explain how cells develop, adapt, become diseased or respond to treatment.
Comparing cells with different histories could reveal sequences of activity associated with different outcomes. Researchers would gain a way to connect a cell’s past with its present.

sources.who: Lirong Zheng, Changyang Linghu and collaborators
sources.showed: They built CytoTape, which stores histories of gene activity along protein threads inside cells. It recorded selected activities over weeks and also worked in living mouse brain.
sources.quote: We demonstrate its utility across multiple mammalian cell types, achieving simultaneous recording of five transcription factor activities and gene transcriptional activities.
sources.cited_for: Selected gene activities can leave lasting, readable histories within individual cells.
sources.not_established: This does not establish accurate histories of diverse biochemical activities together, including metabolism and internal signals.

sources.who: Christopher D. Reinkemeier, Randall J. Platt and collaborators
sources.showed: They built recordanelles, artificial compartments in human cells that collect messenger RNA, the molecules carrying gene instructions. They sampled up to 90% of these RNAs and protected them for several days.
sources.quote: We further show that transient and dynamic transcriptional responses resulting from inducible promoters or interferon signaling are preserved throughout time within the recordanelle at the single-cell level.
sources.cited_for: A broad range of gene messages can be preserved inside individual human cells for later measurement.
sources.not_established: Preserving gene messages does not establish their precise event order, timing or a combined history of other biochemical activities.

shown: Zheng, Linghu and collaborators reported CytoTape recordings of selected gene activities lasting up to three weeks. Their system also recorded gene activity in living mouse brain.

Reinkemeier, Platt and collaborators preserved a broad range of gene messages in human cells for several days. Together, these approaches demonstrate lasting cellular records with different kinds of coverage.
missing: A recorder must capture gene activity, internal signals and metabolism—the cell’s chemical reactions—together in the same cell.
Reconstructed events need known errors for timing, order, duration and strength throughout the recording period.
Stored histories must remain readable despite limited capacity, information loss and cell growth or division.
The recorder must preserve useful information without substantially changing the cell’s behavior.

milestones.label: Stored histories recover hidden biochemical events
milestones.explanation: Blinded tests would have to recover independently varied signals and metabolic events in individual cells within preset timing, strength and disturbance limits. This would demonstrate the combined capability.

milestones.label: Independent measurements confirm accuracy and detection errors
milestones.explanation: Independent measurements would have to quantify missed events, false detections, channel interference and timing errors, and confirm what indirect signals represent. This would establish whether reconstructed histories are trustworthy.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce the recorder’s operating limits
milestones.explanation: Independent preparations and laboratories would have to reproduce performance across claimed cells and tissues, measuring disturbance, storage loss and recovery of each cell’s history. This would establish reliable operating boundaries.

uncertain: The required activity panel, recording duration, accuracy and success rate still need agreed thresholds.
How much recording can a cell tolerate before its relevant behavior changes?
Links between earlier events and later outcomes would still need experiments to establish cause and effect.

page.title: Multiplexed molecular recording of cellular biochemical histories
page.definition: An intracellular recorder preserves selected histories of transcription (RNA production), signaling and metabolic flux (reaction rates) in the same living cell for later readout. The record yields event identity, order, timing, duration and magnitude with measured errors.

goal.need: In HEK293T cells exposed to 50 ng/ml doxycycline for 20 h, an engineered RNA-storage compartment retained evidence of induction after the ordinary RNA readout had returned to baseline. Such storage bridges the delay between a transient event and cell collection. Recovering event timing and other biochemical activities requires additional recording capabilities.

figures.caption: Reporter RNA after withdrawal of doxycycline
figures.note: HEK293T mCherry::ms2 reporter; quantitative PCR; three biological replicates. RNA retention does not establish timestamp resolution.

completion.title: One recorder recovers quantitative transcriptional, signaling and metabolic histories in the same cell.
completion.criterion: An independently replicated living-cell demonstration uses intracellular storage and endpoint readout to reconstruct transcriptional, signaling and metabolic-flux histories together in individual cells. Decoding distinguishes reversed event orders and short, strong inputs from long, weak inputs. Independent time-resolved measurements validate reconstructed onset, duration and magnitude and quantify recording-induced changes in the measured physiology. The tested input panel, recording interval and errors delimit the claim; no universal numerical acceptance limits have been published.
completion.basis: Searches covered NIH recording award targets, the DOE microbial-design report, ENGRAM protocols, developer perspectives, and standards, prize and registered-protocol benchmarks. No source defined an acceptance test combining these three activity classes or limits for duration, reconstruction error and cellular disturbance. This Atlas fallback combines the stated goals with the minimum requirement that timing and intensity be distinguishable; it is not an agreed field standard.

milestones.title: A DNA recorder detects regulatory activity at least twice that of minimal-promoter controls.
milestones.criterion: In mammalian cells, stored DNA edits identify activity of a cis-regulatory element, a DNA sequence controlling transcription. The ENGRAM protocol uses activity at least twice that of minimal-promoter-only controls, with statistics accounting for independent barcodes and replicates; its authors describe this cutoff as subjective. Related result, published on 17 July 2024: NF-κB and WNT recorders achieved 19.0-fold and 22.6-fold ranges above unstimulated controls after 48 h at maximal tested doses, respectively, in three integration replicates. These controls differ from the protocol's minimal-promoter benchmark.
milestones.set_by: Nathans and colleagues, ENGRAM protocol, control-selection guidance; a developer heuristic for mammalian DNA recording.
milestones.threshold_quote: However, as a subjective ballpark, we look for activity at least two-fold greater than minP negative controls.

milestones.title: A single-cell recorder recovers the sequence and timing of two signaling pathways.
milestones.criterion: Recover the sequence and timing of two signaling pathways simultaneously in single cells, as specified in the NIH-funded project summary. Related result, published on 17 July 2024: ENGRAM–DNA Typewriter distinguished 15 temporal Tet-On/WNT stimulation programmes in HEK293T populations, each run in three integration replicates and read after 6 days. These population measurements do not establish the project's single-cell target.
milestones.set_by: UCLA project R35GM162272, funded by NIH/NIGMS; project-specific target in the HHS TAGGS project summary.
milestones.threshold_quote: simultaneous recording of the sequence and timing of two signaling pathways.

milestones.title: Recordings of three developmental pathways link earlier signaling to cell fate in embryo models.
milestones.criterion: Mouse embryonic stem cells record BMP, Wnt and Nodal activity; stem-cell-derived embryo models and chimeric embryos connect earlier signaling windows to cell fate and spatial organization at the onset of organogenesis. Related in vivo result, published on 26 January 2026: CytoTape-vivo recovered Fos-promoter histories from 14,123 CA1 neurons in one mouse fixed on day 18. That experiment establishes tissue recording but does not establish the three-pathway developmental target.
milestones.set_by: UCLA project R35GM162272, funded by NIH/NIGMS; the HHS TAGGS summary specifies mouse embryonic stem cells, embryo models and chimeric embryos.
milestones.threshold_quote: record three key developmental pathways: BMP, Wnt, and Nodal.

milestones.title: Separately validated recorders recover transcriptional, signaling and metabolic-flux histories.
milestones.criterion: Intracellular recorders separately recover time-ordered transcriptional, signaling and metabolic-flux histories in living-cell experiments. For each activity class, independent measurements establish how stored records encode timing, duration and magnitude, including sensor and writing delays. This precursor establishes the three calibrated recording functions before their combination within the same cell.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; searches of NIH targets, the DOE report and recorder protocols found no published cross-class precursor test.

not_found: No standards, prize or registered-protocol benchmark was found defining completion for combined transcriptional, signaling and metabolic recording.
No external acceptance test was found for the cross-class precursor in m4.
No opened source demonstrated calibrated histories of all three activity classes together in individual cells.

results.detail: This demonstrates spatially resolved recording in living tissue, but does not record BMP, Wnt and Nodal in embryo models or link their signaling histories to developmental fate.

results.finding: CytoTape recorded two sequential Fos-promoter responses over 21 days in 10 cultured neurons.
results.detail: The transcriptional recorder resolved sequential events and reported waveform features, but the source does not establish separately calibrated recorders for all three activity classes, including metabolic flux.

results.finding: Human-cell recordanelles sampled up to 90% of endogenous mRNAs; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The source reports preservation of transient and dynamic transcriptional responses at single-cell resolution. It does not establish calibrated, time-ordered transcriptional, signaling and metabolic-flux recording across all three activity classes.
results.quote: We demonstrate that the recordanelle can be engineered to recruit engineered RNAs or a sampling of up to 90% of all endogenous mRNAs and protect them over several days. We further show that transient and dynamic transcriptional responses resulting from inducible promoters or interferon signaling are preserved throughout time within the recordanelle at the single-cell level.

results.finding: In K562 cells, a high-activity CRE recorded across two barcodes and three integration replicates was 23.6-fold above the minimal-promoter control.
results.detail: Barcode counts were summed by construct before fold differences were calculated; significance was assessed with a two-tailed t-test.
results.quote: Barcodes corresponding to the highly active CRE were 41.3-fold, 23.6-fold, and 15.1-fold more abundant than barcodes corresponding to promoter-less, minP-only or lowly active CRE controls, respectively.

results.finding: FPTT recorded sequential STAT3 and NFAT responses in single HEK293T cells; sample size not reported; each stimulation lasted 8 hours.
results.detail: Sequential IL-6 and KCl treatments produced distinguishable pathway activity patterns; reversing their order produced a different pattern.
results.quote: Furthermore, when the cells were first stimulated with IL-6 (500 ng/ml) for 8 hours and then switched to stimulation with KCl (45 mM) for another 8 hours (fig. S36D), a clear asynchronous response could be observed between IL-6–dependent red patterns (STAT3 activity) and KCl-dependent green patterns (NFAT activity)

results.finding: In 110 mouse gastruloids, Wnt activity at 96 hours predicted later anterior-posterior cell positions.
results.detail: Separate mESC lines recorded Wnt, Nodal or BMP activity; early Nodal and BMP recordings also predicted later spatial position. The study did not record all three pathways in the same cells or report chimeric embryo experiments.

results.finding: GEMINI recorded NF-κB-mediated transcription in HEK cells (n=106, 79 and 47 particles), with an approximately 2-hour activation delay.
results.detail: The recorder captured ordered activation and deactivation and dose-dependent amplitudes. The source does not establish separately calibrated metabolic-flux recording, and signaling is measured through transcriptional output.
